Appreciate the questions — short answers + proposed config approaches below. See attached policy example for concrete YAML snippets (model_routing_policy_example.yaml).

1) Model routing for mixed latency/cost workloads:
- Primary path for interactive chat: keep requests on a low-latency model (e.g., redwood/gpt-large-16k-8q) pinned to US region with SST-enabled kernels.
- Fallback chain: on high-load or cost constraint, automatically route to a medium-cost model (redwood/gpt-medium-8k-4q) or a local cached completion derived from prefix/KV cache.
- Policy example: route by request.tags.latency_priority -> if high then prefer low-latency model; else prefer cost-optimized. Also add capacity-tier routing: dedicated pool -> hosted general -> burst to reserve.

2) Structured output & tool-calling:
- Redwood supports JSON schema-constrained structured output and function/tool calling semantics (similar to function-calling). We validate outputs and can enforce schema constraints server-side or via client SDK.
- Best practice: return a top-level JSON object, include a schema_version field, and use post-processing checks for strict types.

3) Embeddings + reranker:
- Recommended embedding model: redwood/emb-2-small for dense reranking (cost-effective), or emb-3 for higher recall.
- Reranker approaches: a) simple: embed candidates + use vector similarity; b) reranker model: run a small cross-encoder on top of top-K (recommended for precision). Redwood can host the reranker as an inference route or you can run it in your infra and call Redwood for embeddings.

Sample policy snippet (high-level):
- name: acme-chat-policy
  conditions:
    - request.type == "interactive" and request.latency_priority == "high"
  route:
    primary: redwood/gpt-large-16k-8q@us-east-1
    fallback: redwood/gpt-medium-8k-4q@us-east-1
    cache: prefix_kv: on
    health-check: p99_latency < 350ms

I attached a full example YAML and a short note on fallback chain behavior. Happy to walk through it in the workshop.

— Marcus

Quick technical add-on from the integration side — some pragmatic notes to speed the POC.

Auth & SDK:
- Hosted API: API keys are the quickest path for POC. Keys scoped per-environment and support rotation via the Console.
- Private/Dedicated: OIDC + mTLS supported for private control plane; recommend mTLS for PCI-scope flows.
- SDKs: we have official JS/Python/Go clients. Example (JS) quickstart: 

// JS quickstart (pseudocode)
import Redwood from '@redwood/inference';
const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY, region: 'us-east-1' });
const resp = await client.chat.create({ model: 'redwood/gpt-large-16k-8q', input: '...' });

Routing & caching:
- Use request-level metadata (tags) to influence routing decisions (latency_priority, cost_tier, region_pref).
- Enable prefix_kv caching for sessioned chats — can reduce token-level costs by 20-40% depending on reuse.
- For embeddings batch jobs: use the batch embeddings endpoint with CSV input to reduce per-request overhead.

Compliance evidence:
- We can share SOC2 report and encryption architecture docs during the workshop. For PCI we recommend isolating cardholder flows to a dedicated path with stronger auth (mTLS) and dedicated logging retention.

Links: HubSpot deal + sample Drive folder are in Marissa's email. I can post the example policy YAML to the Drive after this thread.
